summary: Well-known issues have prevented deployment of multicast on 802.11 (Wi-Fi) and other local wireless networks. This informational document describes limitations of wireless layer 2 multicast, the enhancement features specified by IETF and IEEE 802, and operational choices that improve performance, with recommendations.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending one message to many devices over Wi-Fi works badly. This document explains why and offers tips to make it work better.

questions: why is multicast slow on wifi
subtitle: Why multicast fails on Wi-Fi and what to do about it.

tldr.problem: Sending one message to many devices over Wi-Fi works much worse than wired networks because Wi-Fi multicast uses low transmission rates, has no error recovery, and consumes network capacity. This breaks protocols that rely on multicast for discovery and control.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the fundamental Layer 2 issues (reliability, data rates, capacity, power consumption), how higher-layer protocols are affected, and technical solutions like proxy ARP, buffering, converting multicast to unicast, and GroupCast with Retries.
tldr.outcome: Multicast over wireless remains problematic and not widely deployed. Operators must choose between deploying workarounds, designing protocols to avoid multicast, or accepting the performance penalties.

today: RFC 9119 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. Multicast remains problematic on wireless networks, and the solutions described in the RFC are not universally deployed.

sections.title: The Multicast Problem on Wireless
sections.content: Well-known issues prevent deployment of multicast on 802.11 (Wi-Fi) and other wireless local-area networks. Unlike wired Ethernet, where multicast and unicast have similar costs, wireless has fundamental constraints that make multicast expensive. Multicast is used for control messages in many protocols: Neighbor Discovery, address resolution, service discovery, and on-demand routing. Modern applications also use multicast for video delivery and Push To Talk services. The RFC describes limitations at Layers 2 and 3, along with enhancement features designed by IETF and IEEE 802 to ameliorate the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Many network protocols need to send one message to lots of devices at once. Wi-Fi makes this really hard, so the document explains what goes wrong and how to fix it.

sections.title: Why Wireless Multicast is Unreliable
sections.content:
Wireless multicast has three fundamental limitations at Layer 2. First, multicast frames are not acknowledged. When the AP sends a unicast frame, the device replies with an ACK; the AP retransmits if it does not get an ACK. Multicast frames cannot receive ACKs from multiple devices, so the AP never knows if they arrived and cannot retransmit. This causes high packet error rates, often 5% or more.

Second, multicast uses the basic rate—the slowest rate supported by the slowest connected device. To ensure all devices receive the frame regardless of distance from the AP, the AP transmits at a low modulation and coding scheme. This occupies the medium much longer than unicast to nearby devices. Unicast rates can be up to Gbps, while multicast might be a few Mbps, creating a 3-order-of-magnitude difference in transmission time.

Third, multicast transmission at higher power increases interference. To reach all devices, multicast transmissions use higher power and occupy more spectrum area, creating interference in neighboring cells and reducing airtime available for other traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Wi-Fi does not check if multicast messages get through. It has to use a super-slow speed so everyone hears it, which wastes the radio's airtime. It also sends stronger signals that interfere with nearby networks.

sections.title: Layer 3 Issues and Protocol Impact
sections.content:
Higher-layer protocols suffer when multicast is unreliable. IPv6 makes heavy use of multicast for Neighbor Discovery: IPv6 addresses change frequently for privacy, so Neighbor Solicitation messages flood the network for duplicate address detection and address lookup. Router advertisements are also periodically multicast.

Service discovery protocols like mDNS (used for finding printers) also rely on multicast. When many devices register with mDNS simultaneously, they saturate the wireless link and degrade the network. Additionally, spurious traffic from Internet backscatter and scanning causes routers to broadcast ARP requests. On wired networks this is tolerable, but on wireless it wakes power-saving devices unnecessarily, draining batteries.

Power-save mode creates another problem: every station must wake up to receive multicast frames, even if it does not want them. The AP cannot know which stations are interested in which multicast groups, so all must wake.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols that depend on multicast (like finding out if an IPv6 address is already taken) end up flooding the wireless network and wasting power because devices have to wake up for messages they do not care about.

sections.title: Solutions: Protocol Enhancements and Operational Choices
sections.content:
Proxy methods reduce multicast on the air: Proxy ARP (in 802.11-2012) allows the AP to answer ARP requests on behalf of associated stations, keeping ARP off the wireless medium. IPv6 Proxy Neighbor Discovery (in 802.11-2012) does the same for IPv6 address resolution. These require no changes to stations.

Buffering and power save: The AP buffers multicast frames and sends them after a DTIM (Delivery Traffic Indication Map) beacon, allowing power-saving stations to wake at a known time. However, this delays multicast and limits the number of buffered frames.

Converting multicast to unicast avoids most wireless multicast problems. Layer 2 conversion maps multicast groups to individual unicast frames (using IGMP or MLD snooping to identify which stations want each group). Directed Multicast Service (DMS) lets stations request that the AP convert specific multicast flows to unicast. Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT) encapsulates multicast in unicast for traversal over unicast-only links like Wi-Fi.

GroupCast with Retries (GCR) improves reliability by retransmitting group-addressed frames and using block acknowledgement to learn which devices missed frames. This increases reliability but may add latency.
sections.plainLanguage: Solutions include having the AP answer some messages itself, delaying multicast until devices wake up, converting multicast to individual messages, or retransmitting multicast frames if devices miss them.

sections.title: Deployment Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that future protocols carefully scrutinize their use of multicast over wireless. When multicast is necessary, use proxy methods to conserve bandwidth and power. Design protocols to work with low duty-cycle operation (devices in power-save mode).

Operators should enable proxy methods on APs. For spurious Neighbor Discovery (caused by Internet background radiation), several mitigations exist: ARP Sponges listen for ARP requests and reply for addresses they believe are unused, preventing the router from broadcasting. Routers can implement negative ARP caches, or operators can firewall unused IP space to prevent ARP flooding. In some networks, stateful firewalls or firewalling large unused address ranges have proven effective at large gatherings.

Multicast remains a second-class citizen on wireless networks. While IETF and IEEE 802 have designed enhancements, they are not widely deployed and multicast is often blocked or disabled by operators. Some work remains to resolve the tension between the reliability and efficiency needed for Wi-Fi and the behavior of multicast protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Network designers should avoid multicast on Wi-Fi when possible. If they need it, they should use the proxy features on access points and accept that multicast will not work as reliably as it does on wired networks.
